group.title: Science and the environment
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A scientific test done to discover or prove something.
examples: The students did an {experiment} with magnets.
wrong: An experiment is a fact that nobody needs to test.

words.meaning: A room or building for scientific work.
examples: The samples were tested in a {laboratory}.
wrong: A laboratory is a room where people sleep after dinner.

words.meaning: The act of finding something that was not known before.
examples: The {discovery} of penicillin saved millions of lives.
wrong: A discovery is something everyone already knew about.

words.meaning: A group of animals or plants of the same kind.
examples: This {species} of frog lives only on one island.
wrong: A species is a single animal with no relatives.

words.meaning: No longer existing because all of its kind have died.
examples: Dinosaurs have been {extinct} for millions of years.
wrong: The bird is extinct, so there are thousands in the park.

words.meaning: The natural place where an animal or plant lives.
examples: Cutting down forests destroys the {habitat} of many birds.
wrong: A habitat is the food an animal eats.

words.meaning: All the living things in an area and how they affect each other.
examples: Pollution can damage the whole {ecosystem}.
wrong: An ecosystem is a single tree with nothing living near it.

words.meaning: Gases sent into the air, for example from cars or factories.
examples: The city wants to cut carbon {emissions}.
wrong: Emissions are the clean air in a forest.

words.meaning: Able to be replaced naturally, such as wind or solar power.
examples: The country gets half its power from {renewable} sources.
wrong: Coal is renewable because it runs out.

words.meaning: A fuel like coal, oil or gas, formed from very old plants and animals.
examples: Burning {fossil fuels} adds carbon to the air.
wrong: A fossil fuel is energy from the wind.

words.meaning: A long time with little or no rain.
examples: The {drought} killed most of the crops.
wrong: A drought is a week of heavy rain and floods.

words.meaning: A large amount of water covering land that is usually dry.
examples: The {flood} damaged hundreds of homes.
wrong: A flood is a long time without any water.

words.meaning: Able to continue without harming the environment.
examples: We need {sustainable} ways to grow food.
wrong: The plan is sustainable, so it will destroy the forest soon.

words.meaning: The protection of animals, plants and natural places.
examples: She works in wildlife {conservation}.
wrong: Conservation means cutting down every tree.

words.meaning: The variety of plants and animals in a place.
examples: Rainforests have very high {biodiversity}.
wrong: High biodiversity means only one kind of plant lives there.

words.meaning: The cutting down of large areas of forest.
examples: {Deforestation} is a big problem in the Amazon.
wrong: Deforestation is the planting of new forests.

words.meaning: Grown without artificial chemicals.
examples: We buy {organic} vegetables.
wrong: Organic fruit is covered in artificial chemicals.

words.meaning: A chemical used to kill insects that harm crops.
examples: Farmers sprayed {pesticide} on the fields.
wrong: A pesticide is a vitamin for insects.

words.meaning: Using energy from the sun.
examples: We put {solar} panels on our roof.
wrong: Solar power comes from coal mines.

words.meaning: The layer of gases around the earth.
examples: Carbon dioxide traps heat in the {atmosphere}.
wrong: The atmosphere is the rock deep under the ground.

words.meaning: A gas, like carbon dioxide, that traps heat around the earth.
examples: Cars produce {greenhouse gases}.
wrong: A greenhouse gas cools the planet down.

words.meaning: The smallest unit of a substance, made of atoms.
examples: A water {molecule} has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
wrong: A molecule is bigger than a planet.

words.meaning: The smallest living part of a plant or animal.
examples: The human body has billions of {cells}.
wrong: A cell is a very large animal.

words.meaning: A part of a cell that controls what a living thing inherits from its parents.
examples: Eye color is passed on through {genes}.
wrong: Genes are habits you learn at school.

words.meaning: The slow change of living things over many generations.
examples: Darwin wrote about the {evolution} of species.
wrong: Evolution happens in one afternoon.

words.meaning: The force that pulls things toward the earth.
examples: {Gravity} makes the apple fall.
wrong: Gravity makes things float up into the sky.

words.meaning: To move around a planet or star in a curved path.
examples: The moon {orbits} the earth.
wrong: The earth orbits the moon every day.

words.meaning: A tool that makes far objects look closer.
examples: We looked at Saturn through a {telescope}.
wrong: A telescope is a tool for hearing quiet sounds.

words.meaning: A machine sent into space to move around the earth.
examples: The TV signal comes from a {satellite}.
wrong: A satellite is a car that drives on the moon.

words.meaning: To watch something carefully to learn about it.
examples: Scientists {observed} the birds for a year.
wrong: She observed the stars with her eyes closed.

words.meaning: To find the size, amount or degree of something.
examples: {Measure} the room before you buy a carpet.
wrong: I measured the table by guessing its size.

words.meaning: A small amount taken to test or show what the rest is like.
examples: The doctor took a blood {sample}.
wrong: A sample is the whole of something.

words.meaning: Facts and numbers collected to be studied.
examples: We collected {data} from 500 people.
wrong: Data is an opinion with no facts.

words.meaning: A decision you reach after thinking about the facts.
examples: What {conclusion} did you reach?
wrong: The conclusion was the first step of the study.

words.meaning: A substance that makes air, water or land dirty.
examples: The factory released {pollutants} into the river.
wrong: A pollutant makes water cleaner.

words.meaning: Able to be used again after processing.
examples: These bottles are {recyclable}.
wrong: The bag is recyclable, so it must go to landfill.

words.meaning: A place where waste is buried in the ground.
examples: Most plastic ends up in {landfill}.
wrong: A landfill is a clean beach for swimming.

words.meaning: The amount of carbon dioxide a person or activity produces.
examples: Flying less will reduce your {carbon footprint}.
wrong: A carbon footprint is a mark your shoe leaves on the floor.

words.meaning: Wild animals and plants.
examples: The park is home to a lot of {wildlife}.
wrong: Wildlife means pets that live in our homes.

words.meaning: At risk of disappearing completely.
examples: The tiger is an {endangered} species.
wrong: The bird is endangered, so there are millions everywhere.
